utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, everybody, and especially to you, Madam Registrar. If you could kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much. All the accused are present. The Prosecution today is Mr. Thayer, Mr. Vanderpuye. Is there anyone else behind the column or not? No. What happened to Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe before we broke, he indicated he wouldn't be here for the first day. We do expect him back, however, tomorrow, and perhaps around the second session he should be in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. I just ask you for the record. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then from the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Nikolic. That's it, I think. Mr. Lazarevic is here, yes. Mr. Bourgon is here. That's it. So I hope you have recovered your energies and that you also had some time to enjoy together with your respective families. We are reconvened now to what seems to be the tail end of the evidentiary stage of the trial. In the course of the week, you will be approached by our senior legal officer to get some information -- further information, more than you have given already, so that we can plan the schedule accordingly for the next two months. That applies also to the Prosecution, especially if there is a notation to ask for rebuttal and so on and so forth. So we need to plan, and we prefer to plan -- to have the information beforehand and plan ahead, rather than wait and see what happens later. Okay. Today we continue with the last witness of the Miletic Defence team. Are there any preliminaries? None? None. Your estimate for the time -- for the time being, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that 16 hours should be necessary, but I can tell you later during the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you still maintain the 16 hours that you had asked for. I take it you asked for 12 hours, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President, but that will vary depending upon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously. I'm just asking so we plan ahead. All right, let's bring the -- Mr. Thayer, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And happy new year to you and Your Honours. And happy new year to everybody. Mr. President, we did have a very brief preliminary that I alerted our friends to. With all the mirth and merry-making over the holidays with the OTP, we missed the deadline for the Pandurevic motion to amend its 65 ter list of witnesses and exhibits. THE COURT: We are aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We are prepared to file a written response that we do not object to the application. However, we would need to seek leave to reply out of time from the Trial Chamber in order to do that. We've done it both ways. We've provided an oral response to some of these motions in the past, and other times we've filed a written response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's cut it short. I don't think that Mr. Pandurevic -- Mr. Haynes will object to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What about you, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, so permissioned granted, you can register your non-objection orally, and we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the motion is granted, basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you are most welcome to this Tribunal. You have been summoned as an expert witness by the Defence team for General Miletic. Your testimony is going to take quite some time. I think that you should at least earmark the entire week that we've just started, and I wouldn't be surprised if we go into the next one as well. Much depends on how much you succeed in keeping your answers brief and to the point. If you try to answer the question -- the whole question and nothing but the question, the chances are that you will go home earlier than expected. If you beat around the bush and you go around in circles and give lengthy answers when they could be shorter, you will be here for longer than I have told you. Before you start giving evidence, our Rules require you to make a solemn declaration to the effect that you will be testifying the truth. The text has just been handed to you now. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kosovac, do you have a rank? Would you like us to address you with any particular rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't mind any way you wish. You can call me "Mr. Kosovac" or any other way you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Please make yourself comfortable. Madame Fauveau will be asking you questions, and we'll follow up from there. Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please give us your name and surname?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Slobodan Kosovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell us about your education background and what school you completed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: I completed grammar school, which was the highest form of civilian education, and then the military academy and became an officer of the JNA, and then the Command Staff Academy, which would be equal to the Masters of Arts in civilian life. Then I was promoted to colonel, and then I finished the School of National Defence, which is the highest school in the army, equaling a doctorate; and this was a precondition for me to become a general.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell us about your career and tell us the positions that you held?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: I'll try and be brief. In my career, I served in various units of the army, in the General Staff, in the Ministry, and later on -- or, rather, now I'm a civilian in the army units. I served as a commander. I served in the rocket units of the anti-aircraft defence, and also I was the chief -- the assistant chief of the commander for education, and the General staff, I worked in the development, organisation, mobilisation and military duties; and I performed duties from the chief of department, chief of section, and assistant chief of General Staff in the Ministry. I was the assistant in the Ministry for human resources and the executive director of the Ministry. When I was retired, I found a job, a civilian job, and I'm most engaged in strategy, man [as interpreted] and management.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Have you published any books, documents, or papers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: In my career, I've published a number of professional papers, books, and degree papers. My professional papers dealt with military obligation, organisation, management, and the civilian control over the military. My papers have been published by non-governmental organisations, such as the Atlantic Council of Serbia, and they have also been published by the General Staff, the Ministry. And the last papers I've published dealt with the organisation of companies in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You've been hired by the Defence of General Miletic to write a report. Could you briefly tell us what was the purpose of this report?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: What is the purpose of this report? Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was first briefed and then asked to write about the role of General Miletic while he served in the Army of Republika Srpska, with a special reference to the duties that he performed during a given period of time. Based on that, I analysed General Miletic's post, his involvement, his links with the environment, i.e., with the environment of his post, and I also analysed whether General Miletic had other duties that went beyond his post. And as a result of that, I've provided my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell us the sources you used to draft this report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: I've used a number of sources. My main source was the source that I received from you, from the Defence. I also used materials that determined the position and the role of the organ that General Miletic worked for. I also used documents of the Yugoslav People's Army, as well as the documents of the Army of Yugoslavia. I also used the search engines on the internet, and I compared the army with other modern militaries, such as NATO. I also used interviews with my colleagues, be it from the Army of Yugoslavia, or the Army of Republika Srpska, or even the militaries of the former Yugoslav People's Army. I interviewed high-ranking officers from all of these militaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to show you page 5 of your report. It is document 5D759. I'm interested in paragraph 3 on page 5 of both versions. In this paragraph, you wrote: "Despite the fact that everything occurred over 3 [as interpreted] years, they could be seen as dynamic." What do you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thirteen years. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that I am looking at this paragraph, I can say that the event took place almost 14 years ago, because I wrote the report almost a year ago. What I meant was to draw a comparison between life and expert report. In life, new documents appear every day. There's no indication to prove that there will be no new documents, that the public and media are discovering new events. I would like to remind everybody of a series of events that were discovered last year from the point of view of the 5th Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I would also like to remind everybody that many things are being divulged as we speak. For example, people have been -- or remains have been found 15 years after the events. So every expert report that strives to be objective must be open and must be capable of being built up based on new facts, and that may be built into such report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Madame Fauveau-Ivanovic, before we go further, can I know when the General retired?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes. You heard the question from Judge Kwon. Could you please tell us when you retired?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: 2005. 15 September 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What position did you hold at the time of war in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1995, I was just about to finish the School of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Maybe to make things clearer, could you tell us which army you belonged to from 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: From 1992 to the end of my career, I was in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And to finish this issue, finish with this issue, could you tell us when you were promoted to general?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: I became general on the 16th of June, 2000, and lieutenant general on the 16th of June, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to come back to your report, still page 5. On paragraph 2, you said that it is impossible to analyse the events of 1995 without taking into account the events and behaviours of what had happened earlier in that area from 1992 to 1995. I believe there's a mistake in the text, anyway. It's January 1st, 1992, to August 1995. Could you tell us why the events that occurred in this area are absolutely essential to understand what exactly happened in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: First of all, the events that took place in this area, i.e., the most important thing is the clash between the two militaries, in order to analyse a clash between the two militaries, you can't analyse that moment in isolation. How far back will you go is mostly determined by the way these militaries are organised. Because of the way these militaries were organised, you have to go back to the year 1992. That's one aspect. The second aspect, which is very important for my analysis, is the following: No single event happens in isolation, on its own. You have to determine the causality or you have to analyse the causes and the consequences in order to arrive at the beginning of the event that would happen later. And these two elements made me go back in time and research a longer period than the one that was given to me as the task to analyse.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: For the transcript, there is no -- there's no mistake in the report. It is an error in my notes. It is from January 1995 to August 1995. I would now like to start with the beginning, if I can say so, and show you Exhibit P25. This is the minutes of the Assembly meeting of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina in May 12, 1992. I would like to see page 12 in the B/C/S version and page 13 in the English version. I'm interested in the paragraph that's lower on the page, the last paragraph on what we have on the screen. In this paragraph, we see that the Presidency, the Government, the Council for National Security, have formulated strategic priorities, i.e., strategic goals for the Serbian people. According to this document, were you able to determine whether the army was actually involved in the determination and the formulation of these strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: This was created before the 12th of May, as far as I could see. Before the 12th of May, there was no Army of Republika Srpska; hence, theoretically, it was not possible for the military to be involved in the creation of the strategic goals.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: According to the conclusions found on page 1 of this document, from page 1 to 5 of this document, could you tell us whether you were able to determine whether the strategic goals which had been presented during this Assembly were actually adopted?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: The conclusions of this meeting was -- were of some interest to me because of the analyses of the causes and consequences of the organisation of the state and the organisation of the military. I believe that I have studied them in detail, and based on that, I can state that according to the minutes, the strategic goals were not adopted at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 2 of the B/C/S version, which corresponds to page 1 in the English version. Could we have this on the screen, please. It's the last paragraph in English, and regarding the B/C/S version, this is the second paragraph of Article 1, which refers to the setting up of a working group aimed at drawing a map of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Have you ever found such a map?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: No, I've not found such a map. I have not even found any indication of a working version of such a map.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move to page 14 for the English and page 13 for the B/C/S. I'm interested in the paragraph discussing the third strategic goal.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you please read it? It is the third paragraph on the B/C/S page and the second one on the English page.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This third strategic goal deals with the Drina Valley. Could you tell us exactly what is the importance of the Drina Valley for the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: The Drina Valley was a strategic goal for Republika Srpska as well as for Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, there were two different types of interests involved. The goal of Republika Srpska was to prevent this area from being a border between the peoples in Republika Srpska and in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The strategic goal of Bosnia-Herzegovina with respect to this area is to isolate it and to create a border there between the Serbian people and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And the latter strategic goal was partly shared by the Croatian Community in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Militarily-wise, could you tell us whether this strategic objective, as written in these minutes, included the movement of the Muslim population living in the Drina Valley, the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Irrespective of the fact that the Trial Chamber has asked me to be up to the point, I have to provide a somewhat longer answer at the moment. First of all, there's no single military document that can be created based on a proclamation, on an idea, on constitution or some other documents. Every military document has to start with a task that is given to the military, and the task arises from the law, directives at the national level. Second of all, even if somebody were to formulate a strategic goal, as it is, and try to incorporate it into the directive or any other document, it is very precise in itself; and it does not imply any status quo in regulating the situation once the area is conquered.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we now move back to page 13 in English, page 12 for the B/C/S. In the B/C/S version, I'm interested in the bottom of the page. In English, it's the third paragraph from the bottom. At the end of this page in B/C/S, we see the first strategic objective, which is defined as separation from the other two national communities, separation of states. Now, tell us, military-wise, whether this strategic objective included moving the Muslim population out of the territories controlled by Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: The question whether this implies the movement of population is speculation. The separation of states implies the creation of two states and everything that remains in these two states. I don't see a possibility for the separation of state to imply movement of people. People had rights in the former Yugoslavia, and that right was honoured from Slovenia until the very end. And as far as I could understand, this is what the representatives of Republika Srpska also insisted on very strongly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You already answered my next question, but I would like to be very accurate. So could you tell us exactly what was the position of the Croats in Bosnia? And in the meanwhile, I would like to show you also document 5D546. I need the first page in both versions. This is a document from the Regional Community of Herzegovina and Travnik, and the paragraph starting right under "Conclusions," at the end of this paragraph it says, and I quote: [In English] "The Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina finally has to start conducting the decisive and tactic policy which should bring about the realisation of our eternal dream, a joint Croatian state." [Interpretation] This document dates back to November 12, 1991. Could you tell us whether this was the objective of the Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This objective of the Croatian people, is this objective of the Croatian people different from the first objective of the Serbian people that we have just seen in the previous document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: In the previous answer, the implication was of the people in Slovenia, Croatia and elsewhere, and this applies to the people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is a notorious fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina was often called a little Yugoslavia, and there were four strong groups in that state: Muslim, Croat, Serb, and the fourth group were Yugoslavs, and they were very strong. When the former Yugoslavia broke up, the three prevalent peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Muslims, Serbs and Croats, had the same goal, but expressed in three different ways. The Serbs wanted Bosnia-Herzegovina to remain in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and to remain as a state in the former Yugoslavia, and they based their goals on that. If Bosnia-Herzegovina were to be separated, they wanted the Republika Srpska to be separated as well and be joined with the Federal Yugoslavia. Muslims had their different goal, and Croats insist, which is visible in this document, on two steps. The first step would be to create -- or, rather, to separate Bosnia-Herzegovina from Yugoslavia and to be independent, and the second step would be for Croatia -- for Croatian people to form their banovina which would be joined with the Republic of Croatia, which means that the goals of Serbs and Croats overlapped, but from different directions, one from the left direction and the other from the right direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to show you some documents from the army of the Army of Republika Srpska from that period of time, 1992, and first of all I'd like to show you 5D962. While we're waiting for this document, this is an order from the Main Staff from 23rd of June, 1992. In this document, I'd like to show you point number 2. This is page 2 both in B/C/S and in English. Could you please read this item, the task of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: If I look at this paragraph 2, I can tell that the Army of Serbian Republic of BH received a total of six tasks, which is only to be expected at a time of war. The first is to deblock roads. The second is for additional mobilisation, that's what they refer to it as, to engage all able-bodied Serbian population. Mobilisation, additional mobilisation, implies involvement under the law and status in the Army of Republika Srpska. The third task being maintaining the roads that were there already. Task number 4 is to prevent a breakthrough from the Spreca towards the Drina. Number 6 is to secure other roads from [indiscernible]-Han Pijesak-Vlasenica, and that's number 6, yes. That's the other road. Number 5 is to fend off and repel enemy forces from this line. Yes, a total of six tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, again, from a military standpoint, when a soldier receives such a task, is the moving of the Muslim population something that is included as part of the task, as part of those six tasks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska or, for that matter, the JNA or, for that matter, any of the armies that emerged from the JNA throughout these areas never had any tasks, organs or, indeed, manpower to move any population at all. If you don't have the tool, you can't do the job.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now move to document 5D1199. This is the order from the Main Staff from the Army of Republika Srpska, dated 12th August 1992. This is about the region of the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to show you page 2, both in the English and in the B/C/S versions, and this is still item number 2, which is about the tasks given to the Army of Republika Srpska. In English, it's at the very bottom of this page, and then it moves on to page number 3.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This task, amongst others, highlights the protection of the population. How do you, as a military person, read this paragraph? To which population does this paragraph refer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: The protection of the population was something that was done in the JNA, and this was something for everyone who was involved in the fighting, and there was fighting going on here. Everyone involved had to look after the population. Now, how do they go about this? There has to be an early warning about any combat operations. They should control the firing in order to keep any collateral damage down. It's about the ways in which combat operations are performed and brought to an end. This is an ongoing task for all JNA units. Whenever there are operations in areas such as these, one has to look after the population. There was never a task that entailed moving any population group in any way at all or based on anything at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And how do you understand the last part of this task, which talks about humanitarian aid and supply of humanitarian aid that is given to the people in all the endangered areas? Of what people -- what people are they talking about in this particular task?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: If you read the task as phrased here, as it relates to humanitarian aid, you see this thing about the legal and planned distribution of humanitarian aid. Then at first you think that the phrasing is somewhat verbose, because it might be phrased as follows "distribution of humanitarian aid," and that's that. Nevertheless, at the time we see increasingly these instances where humanitarian aid was abused in a number of ways. "Legal distribution of humanitarian aid" meant making sure that such humanitarian aid as was distributed was real. "Planned" means that distribution was based on a plan. There is no order here concerning humanitarian aid for any particular population group. This applied equally to all the population that was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At the bottom of this page 2, there is a list of objectives for these activities. And then if you move on to page 3, and in English this is actually page 4, throughout this whole page in this order, there is an offer for disarming -- an offer that is made to the Muslim population for disarmament. Could you please explain what it means, "disarmament of the population"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: "Disarmament of the population" in this case must be seen as twofold. One thing is the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, it had a theory on people [as interpreted]. There were different ways people were armed in order to preserve the integrity of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. From that perspective, anyone in the possession of weapons was now called on to surrender their weapons, because there was a unified military now that was made legal, comprising the Army of Republika Srpska and the police. On the other hand, this disarmament and call that was issued also had the following reasons. This was at the time when many, many units of the BH Army and many of their members were dressing up as civilians of women, disguising themselves in order to perform incursions and fight and attack. There is plenty of evidence indicating this. Therefore, the call was for both to disarm.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Well, there's a slight mistake on page 17, line 18. What it says in the transcript is "the theory of the people," but I think you talked about the theory of the armed people.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the following paragraph, they talk about mopping up the villages. Can you please explain, from a military standpoint, what it means to mop up villages? This is somewhere in the middle of the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: In the military sense, to mop up a village is something that is familiar to any military in the world. It means to eliminate all and any enemy soldiers, to eliminate any weapons that are still around and place them under control, as well as ammunition and any military equipment that is still around. That's what it means, to mop up a village.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, in the military terminology, mopping up something, that includes the transfer of a civilian population or moving a civilian population?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: This is pure speculation. I've never come across that, and I'm not sure where this sort of speculation arises from.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to show you P29, Exhibit P29. This is a directive from the Main Staff from 19th of November, 1992. Actually, what I'm interested in here is the task that was given to the Drina Corps by this directive. In English, it's on page 5, and in B/C/S, on page 11 of the document. This paragraph is hard to read. The only sentence that I'm really interested in as part of this task is that according to this directive, the Drina Corps had, as a task, to force the enemy out of the Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas, together with the Muslim population. Now, you've already briefly touched upon the military terminology and the term "population" as part of this terminology, as part of the Yugoslav theory of the armed people, but could you please explain in greater detail how, in this particular context, you construe this sentence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: This is not really legible, the portion that refers to the Drina Corps, but one can sort of make out what it says. The part of the question that you asked me shouldn't be separated from the whole, because down here I see it says "first offer the possibility of disarmament" and all the other alternatives that were given to the Muslim population in the area. The essence of this task is as follows: Any army, when at war, has the foremost task to beat the enemy. The enemy is beaten in three possible ways. A, the enemy is crushed; B, the enemy surrenders and is captured; and, C, the enemy is driven away from the area in question. And this is the alternative that is offered here for the task to be performed. Bearing in mind the experience that arises here, I would point out an anomaly. The 19th of November, 1992, that's directive number 4. A total of four directives, roughly, over a five-month period issued by the Army of Republika Srpska, which means there was a great deal of experience at work here. They realised that the civilian population was often being used as a shield or as a component of the BH Army, and then a possibility was offered for those who were disarmed and who accepted the government that was in place to remain in the area, which was a perfectly legal thing to do and a perfectly fair thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We shall talk later about events which have taken place from 1993 to 1995, but can you please tell us briefly, very briefly, if the events which took place in Srebrenica in July 1995, in Srebrenica and Zepa, can be somehow connected to this directive number 4?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: In order to link up any elements from two different directives, we must first know why a directive came about. There are two primary causes for something like this to come about. One is the situation on the ground and the other is the putative objective. No directive, at least as far as military theory goes, links up with any other directive. Each directive is self-sufficient. It contains a job. It's completed or not. If not, then it's completed in a different way, depending on the causes, obviously. If you look at the situation on the ground, the situation that prevailed at the time, directive number 4, directive number 7 - I mean 1995 - one realises there is nothing like that. There are two entirely different situations on the ground. If you look at the situation that prevailed in the armed forces, these are entirely different situations. If you look at the objectives that were set, these are two entirely different objectives. There would be no logic in the linking up of these two directives in any sense at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to show you now another document that dates from 1993, which is linked to directive number 4. This is document 5D1323, and this is the analysis from the Drina Corps of the operations carried out on the basis of directives 4 and 5. Could we please have page 4 in English and page 3 in B/C/S. Right at the bottom of this page, you have the objectives and tasks of the operation, operation on the basis of directive 4 for the Drina Corps. Could you please have a look at the tasks to be performed by the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In light of your previous answer, maybe this question is irrelevant, but, however, in light of objective and the tasks of the operation, as understood by the Drina Corps, is the transfer of population something that was included in those tasks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: What we see here is an excellent piece of analysis. This is a great link between this document and directive. There are certain features here, but any army in the world knows that whenever an activity is completed, there needs to be some analysis of that activity. If you look at this analysis of the tasks, one sees very clearly what the tasks were for the Army of Republika Srpska in the Drina Corps, purely military tasks that they were facing, and these tasks were then analysed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just before we move to a very different topic, I'd like to show you page 2 in B/C/S and page 2 in English as well, I think. Towards the middle of the page, it reads, in English -- it's at the bottom of what we see on the screen, so it reads: [In English] "The planning operations was organised and planned with the involvement wherever possible of the commanders of subordinate units. Decisions to engage forces in tasks that have been assigned were adopted, in most cases, through the so-called command's complete method of work." [Interpretation] Later on, we shall talk about the various working methods, command's working methods. Now, at this stage, I would only like to ask you if you can say, from what you have seen in your research, what was the working method that was usually used in the units of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Any army, including the Army of Republika Srpska, used the normal method, a normal method means a complete method, and then the commanders are consulted. The use of any other methods would be exceptional and only for exceptional situations. These are driven by necessity, method, and other methods like that, and that's what the sentence would indicate.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, in light of the fact that we started a little late, what time do you think we will have the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My idea was to have the break as scheduled, at 10.30; in other words, in a couple of minutes. But if you're dealing with a topic that will take you a little bit further, we can take it a little bit further. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would like to move on to another topic, so it would be appropriate if we could take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we will have a 25-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madame, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to talk about the establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska. Can you please show the witness Exhibit D754, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 5D754.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is the decision pertaining to the formation of the Army of the Serbian -- the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, in Article 1 it reads: [In English] "The existing territorial defence units and staffs shall be renamed as commands and units of the army, whose organisation and establishment shall be determined by the president of the Republic." [Interpretation] Now, this is a decision dated the 12th of May, 1992. Is this decision really the basis for the establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a prerequisite for any state to establish an army.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Pursuant to Article 3 of this decision, General Ratko Mladic was to be appointed as commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. Did General Mladic in the Army of Republika Srpska have the Supreme Command and authority?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: It's not easy to see that, based on this decision, but I will try to shed light on that. General Mladic was commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, but he was therefore commander of the Army of Republika Srpska. He was the supreme authority in that army, and he was responsible for everything that the army was doing for everything that was going on. Nevertheless, General Mladic did have a commander who was above him, the supreme commander, who had the authority to exercise command over that army in keeping with all the military and other rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to show you the Constitution of Republika Srpska. This is Exhibit 5D752. So this is the Constitution from December 1992, and I would like to have page 8 in B/C/S and page 18 in English. In Article 106, it says that the president of the Republic commands with the Army of Republika Srpska at times of peace and war. Now, who were the -- what were the authorities of the president of the Republic as compared with that of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: I think there's another section that Article 106 comprises. I think there's something else too --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... show the following page in B/C/S, i.e., page 19 -- sorry, page 9, and this goes throughout the whole page.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: This is the type of army and the type of command where the army is placed directly under the supreme commander. And based on the previous paragraph, an enormous authority is given to the supreme commander. When I say "an enormous amount of authority," I mean the civilian authorities were under too much of a burden, given this phrasing. But this is a practice that occurs all over the world and can be considered as normal. You can see here that the president of the Republic promotes or dismisses the military officers. It's all within his authority, in keeping with the law. He sets up military courts and exercises command over the army. When one exercises command over the army, then one knows that one is responsible for the army, from the planning stage all the way up to the control stage. All of the command basis are in the hands of the Republic [as interpreted]; the planning, the organisation, the control, the personnel policies, and all the supervision.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to show you Exhibit 5D757.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am sorry to interrupt. I just wondered if the witness could slow down a little bit. I hear the translation is being rushed and it's a little difficult for me to keep up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. I think that's the case and if we could slow down, not too particularly, I mean it's the witness. What happens here generally is what you say needs to be translated into English and into French, and that is not an easy job. So if you could slow down a little bit. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just bring a correction to the transcript. This is page 25 and line 8 and 9. I think you said that all the functions of command were in the hands of the president of the Republic. The word "president" is not shown in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, the exhibit that is now on the screen is the order from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska from 18th of August, 1992, about the establishment and the organisation of the Army of Republika Srpska. Now, there are just a few things on which I'd like to focus in this particular order. First of all, this order refers to a decision by the president of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina from 15th of June, 1992, and then it refers to information number 111.901.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction of the interpreter, 111.900.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Before asking you a question, I would like to see that in your report. There is a paragraph 45, which refers to this formation and at some point, you use the acronym "LRF." Can you please explain to us what this formation 111.900 is about and then what this "LRF" acronym means? Now, this paragraph 45 that I'm referring to is on page 17 of the B/C/S version and on page 22 of the English version. This is not this exhibit, it's the other exhibit, but I don't think it's necessary to show it. This is Exhibit 5D759 of the expert report.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: In order to understand how an army is organised, and based on how an army is organised in order to understand the authorities, rights, and responsibilities of an officer or any person who is part of that system, I had to first analyse how an army was organised from scratch. In the previous diagram, we saw an order to organise the army. Its preamble invokes a decision by the president of the Republic of Srpska. It's a decision that I had never seen, knowing, nevertheless, that between the Constitution and the order to organise an army, there is always a decision by the supreme commander called "the foundations of the organisation of an army," or something like that, one may therefore assume that a document like that was never found. One can also infer, with an almost 100 percent probability, given the fact that the army was functioning, that the command did exercise control over the army, that there was such a thing as a supreme commander. There was the defence ministry, and the whole order was complied with. There was this order to organise the army, which also defined the Main Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska. The organisation or the structure of the Main Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska is defined by a book that is called "Establishment." The book is shown over there. It had a number. I don't quite remember what that number was. This book called "Establishment" is a document defining with precision the structure of an organisational unit, its manpower and manning level, their hierarchy, their subordination, and it also defines or determines elements that such an establishment post carries. It also determines any personal weapons that belong to that establishment post. The abbreviation "LRF3" is a form that is used to write up this establishment. The abbreviation stands for "Personal wartime establishment, form number 3." At the time in the Army of Republika Srpska, one used the same type of documents as in the Army of Yugoslavia. Somewhere around that time, the forms were changed. Therefore, if you look at the establishment book, and this is something that has been submitted, you will see that sometimes you will find "LRF3" and in some other places you will find "LRF9." However, in terms of their structure, the forms are identical, making sure that the establishment could always be understood in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: May I now show you this book of establishment. This is 5D758, and this exhibit unfortunately has not been translated. It's of poor quality. Actually, this is a form. Now, this document which you now can see, is this about this establishment you just talked about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Can we now show to the witness page 13 of this document. This document has not been translated, and I would now therefore ask you to explain what these different columns are and what they mean. In other words, what can you see in the first column?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: These columns ensure that complete information is provided on the organisation in the establishment. It would be easier to explain if we could zoom out a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a smaller version, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, like this, that's fine. In the first column is the name of the post. This is the exact name of the establishment post, and each one has a code. This means that job descriptions can be provided by means of a code, so no organisation can invent its own posts. The names of the organisational units at a lower level are also included in the columns, so each post is precisely described, and no other job description can be used other than the one described here in the establishment, because based on the title of the post, the competences of the appropriate commander are also described in the establishment. In the next column, we have the number of posts. If desk officer, for example -- there are three desk officers somewhere, then we have the number 3 here, and then the military/evidentiary specialty or the occupational specialty describes the training that is needed for the particular post or job description. There are five numbers. The first numbers -- the first two numbers refer to whether someone is a private, or an officer, or a non-commissioned officer. If there is a 3, it has to be an officer, if there is a 2 it has to be a non-commissioned officer. Then the next numbers refer to the branch of service, and then -- or the arm of service, in fact, and then we have the training and education needed. For example, we can see that the person has to be an officer, that he can belong to any arm of service, and that he has to have the national --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: He has to have the National Defence School training or education.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. General, please slow down a little bit. Thank you. By the way, do you speak in English at all, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the rank, there is the column "Position group." That is an element designating the rank and level of the commander, and this is used to determine the salary later on. Then the next two columns refer to weapons, personal or common weapons, joint weapons that belong to that establishment post. So we can see here clearly that the commander is entitled to a pistol. Then there are some other numbers which do not belong to the establishment, but were written in by whoever was using the document. And then we have "Transport," means of transport of vehicles, whether a trailer is required, livestock, and main means of communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Court about the groups of positions, how these groups were determined?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: The groups of positions or posts were established by law. The law regulated that every post is described inter alia by the position group. The number of the position group, the smaller it is, the more complex the post and the higher level the post. So here we can see the commander has the position group 2. The disposition of the position groups for the other establishment posts is defined by special criteria. Nowhere in the documentation have I found the defined criteria. However, when this is compared to the disposition of the position groups in the Army of Republika Srpska with the positions that I actually found, I concluded that the same criterion was used as in the Army of Yugoslavia. This criterion ensures that throughout the army, there is a single way of defining the character of every post according to its position in the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And just before we move to the law about the army, you said that the position group for the commander is 2. Can you please say -- can you please read from this document what is the position group for the head of the main -- of the staff, for the staff head?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, Chief of Staff, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: There is no chief of the Main Staff. There is the chief of the staff of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. It's a little bit complicated, but the hierarchy of the units and the sequence of units has been respected here. If you look at the organisational unit staff, the Chief of Staff, who is the deputy of the commander, has position group 3. He has to be a general, and he can be from any arm of service or any service, but he has to be an officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Below this part, it mentions the administration in charge of operational affairs and education. Can you read the position group or the head of administration in charge of operational affairs and education?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: To facilitate understanding, I will read all the elements to you. The chief of the Administration for Operational Affairs and Education is an officer from an arm of service who has the National Defence School and who can be granted the rank of a colonel or a major general, and according to some criteria, I would say that this belongs to the sixth position group. It could be the fifth or the sixth, but I think that according to the criteria, it would be the sixth group.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to show you Exhibit 5D753, which is the law pertaining to the Army of Republika Srpska. This is a law dated from 1st of June 1992. I would like to have article 179, which is on page 17 in B/C/S and page 67 in English. Paragraph 2 gives a number of criteria in order to ascertain the position groups, and in paragraph 1, which is on the previous page in the English version, it says how the salary of officers is determined. Now, one sees in paragraph 2 -- paragraph 2 mentions the tasks granted to an officer given to his position, his responsibilities and other criteria. Now, what about the criteria listed here in the law of Republika Srpska; are these the usual criteria, the ones that you have also seen in the Army of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: These are almost the same criteria as I used in any army. Here, it is specifically stated that the formation is a special position group, and it says on the basis of what the criteria to be established for each such group. What I have seen from the document with the establishment of the JNA, because I have had opportunity to see those, and those of the Army of Republika Srpska, the Army of Yugoslavia, the BH Army, and the establishment of the Macedonian Army, the criteria are so similar that one might say they're actually identical.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you please now refer to Article 177, which is on this same page, a little further up on the page, and in English it's on page 66. We see the criteria determining the salary. The first of this criteria is the rank. Could you tell us the importance of rank in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: As in any army, the hierarchy and subordination are reflected inter alia in the ranks, and these ranks made it easier to determine the position of every individual within the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have page 1 of this document, please, page 1 in B/C/S, which corresponds to page 2 in the English version. I'm interested in Article 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We see that there can be superior officers, subordinate officers, as well as senior or junior officers. Could you please take a look at paragraph 3 of Article 4. It's on the other page at the very top in the B/C/S version. Here, there is a definition of a senior officer, a brief definition. But I'm a layperson, so I would like you to explain exactly what is a senior officer in a unit. Could you tell us exactly what is the function of this person?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: This is one of the universal rules or standards, whatever you choose to call them. It's difficult to resolve the issue of subordinates and superiors. This is something that exists in any organisation. We all know who is boss and who isn't. Regardless of this, military systems are very peculiar and they work under different conditions. They are based on a firm hierarchy and subordination. They must deal with issues such as the following: For example, you have persons in the same place between whom there is no relationship of subordination. In a situation like that, you have to know who is the first in command and who is the second. So this is what senior and junior means. The criterion for defining senior and junior is defined here in a simple way. If you have a number of officers in the same place separated by nothing in terms of hierarchy, the most senior officer among those will be the highest-ranking officer. If they all have the same ranks, the officer with the highest responsibility or duty will be charged in that group. And this is how they make sure that there is always some form of hierarchy, even if purely for the sake of protocol.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to show you another document, 5D751. It's not translated in the system, but we have the translation here at hand. This is the service regulations for the armed forces. This is a document that comes from the JNA. I would like to show you page 17 in the B/C/S, item 37, on page 1 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could the translation be put on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it is already, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Ah, yes, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In paragraph 37, item 2, the following is written --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before you proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm sorry for interrupting. Our device here for the ELMO and e-court, et cetera, is out of commission, so I can't see what's on the ELMO or in e-court; and I wondered if my colleague might have an extra hard copy of the translation for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have an extra copy? If you don't, I can give him mine and I can share -- I can follow on the ELMO, myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I do appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In item 2, paragraph 37 of this regulation, it states, and I quote: [In English] "If their superior officer is absent and prompt measures need to be taken to ensure the fulfillment of urgent tasks, particularly in combat, emergency situations or in restoring disrupted work organisation and prescribed order and discipline, persons serving in the armed forces must carry out orders issued by the most senior officer present." [Interpretation] Was this rule also applied in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. This rule was applied in the Army of Republika Srpska. This is a rule that is applied in any army, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to now show you document P417. This is the service manual -- temporary service manual for the Army of Republika Srpska, dated August 1992. And we need page 10 on the screen, page 10 in both versions. I would like to have item 2 on the screen, at the very bottom of the page in B/C/S. The rule that we see drafted here, could you tell us whether it reflects the previous rule that we saw in the previous document that was a JNA document and it had to do with the senior officer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, essentially it's the same thing. There is no need for me to add anything. But the previous one was a little more specific in detail. However, they both reflect this senior/junior relationship.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Practically, according to the information you had, could you tell us whether, in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, if the commander and the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff were absent, who would have been the senior officer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: What you just said, when you talk about them being absent, you need to be more specific. There is a rule that says a commander is always in his unit, even when a command is not in the room. For example, if the commander of the Army of Republika Srpska and the chief of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska happen not to be in an area, yet all of the other officers of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska are there, then one knows exactly who the most senior officer is. Establishment-wise, it is the chief of the sector for morale, legal and religious affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In -- could General Miletic have been the senior officer in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska in a given circumstance?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: There is a possibility and there is a model that he could have been seen as the most senior officer in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, General Miletic or the head of Administration for Teaching and Operations, but this would be, as it were, a headless model or a pointless model.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let me now move to your report, item 5D759. I need page 15 in the B/C/S version and page 18 in the English. Could you tell us exactly what this organisational chart represents?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: This is a diagram of the organisational structure of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. It represents four levels. Whenever you see a diagram like this, you can always find out what the elements are of each of these organisational units, what the hierarchy is, and how the links and relations between the various organisational units operate.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In paragraph 38 on page 16 of the B/C/S version, and page 20 of the English version, you state that this organisational chart shows the order and sometimes -- and in some places also the rank. So could you tell us what is the meaning of the order and what is the meaning of the rank in this organisational chart? And if we could have the organisational chart back on the screen, page 18 for the English and 15 for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the fact that, as I was reading certain materials, I realised that there was a huge problem concerning the understanding of this relationship, this senior/junior, subordinate/superior representation and standing in for, from the beginning of this expert report I wanted to indicate something that I have chosen to call "rank and order." Before moving on to this diagram, we could talk about ranks, first rank, second rank, first row, second row, in a sense, you might call them, and so on and so forth. As far as "order" is concerned, we might apply that name to the columns, the vertical categories within that rank or order. I wanted to show that in this diagram in two ways; one being the size of the square that stands for an organisational unit. If you look at the diagram, it's easy to see. And the other way is to use colour to mark that. However, these documents were not scanned in colour, although originally they were produced in colour, so this is now moot. That's how I did it, and now I'll try to explain the diagram. At the very top of the system, you see the commander. The first rank is represented by the staff, the sectors, and the independent administrations. Within that rank, you see their order. It's clearly reflected in the diagram. This rank and this order are deduced from two documents, one being the establishment book, which is something that we've been looking at, and it has been shown, and the other being the organisation/mobilisation development book which is not in existence, unfortunately, nor indeed has it been reconstructed, as it were. The second rank is the blue boxes or squares. They are smaller than the sectors, the second row, and you can see that we have the teaching and operations administration. We see all of the branches there and all of the organisational units. So this is the order, and all the other administrations have departments, and the sector for security and information has two administrations. This is displayed on two levels, and the third one shows the administrations within -- the departments within the administrations.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you give us the -- explain the difference between the Main Staff and the Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Certainly. If you look at the diagram, you see that the Main Staff is an organisational unit comprising the staff, the sectors, and the dependent administrations with all its units. The Staff is an organisational unit within the Main Staff. It has its own pre-defined authorities or areas of authority. That is why it is often unacceptable to speak of the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. There is no such position. There is the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could, I just wanted -- I think the translation is mistaken or erroneous, and page 39 looks like line 1. I think the distinction that the expert was drawing was one referring to the Chief of Staff of the army, as distinct from the Chief of Staff of the staff. I think that's not properly recorded in the record on page 39, line 1. If I'm mistaken, just please let me know, but I think that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could we have a confirmation of that from you, General, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My apologies. Could we have a confirmation of that from you, General, please? You follow what Mr. Vanderpuye has just pointed out? What we have on the transcript at line 1 of page 39 is -- or thereabouts: "This is why it is often unacceptable to speak of the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. There is no such position. There is the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska," which read together are a contradiction in terms. Madame, I suggest you handle it straight away.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you please slowly repeat what you said earlier? What is the position that does not exist in the Army of Republika Srpska? Slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Before I say it, we should go back to the previous page, "Establishment," and then I'll tell you what does not exist. In the Army of Republika Srpska, there is no chief of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And can you now tell us what was the function of General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: What exists is Chief of Staff of the staff, of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and we can look at the establishment diagram so I can point it out to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please display page 5D758. Page 13 of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Madame Fauveau. Can I draw your attention to page 31, line 7. I wonder whether that's a misinterpretation as well. Here it is recorded that there is no chief of the staff; there is chief of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe this was a translation error, but I did not pick it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can confirm with the witness again on this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On page 31, line 7, we have the following sentence in the transcript: [In English] "There is no chief of the staff. There is the chief of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska." [Interpretation] The sentence that I just read you, can you tell us whether the sentence I just read you corresponds to what you exactly said?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: I'm getting dizzy from all these definitions, and I can imagine what's going on with you. In order to resolve this problem, can you please put the establishment of the Main Staff on the screen, and whatever errors have been made I think should be clarified forever.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have document 5D758 on the screen, please. Page 13, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's sufficient. I will try to tell you now about what this diagram shows and what gives rise to this dilemma. You can see duty here, Chief of Staff, who is also a deputy commander. This Chief of Staff is in the staff, and this staff is in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. Awkward, but true, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe the witness could mark this document so we see where exactly it is the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you please mark this document and circle "Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska"? It's at the very top of the page. Could you circle it, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: This is the order in which it should be read, Chief of Staff, 2, and in the staff, in the Main Staff of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: For everything could be clear, could you tell us exactly what number 1 corresponds to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Number 1 means Chief of Staff who is also deputy commander. This is Colonel General Milovanovic's duty. Number 2 means the Chief of Staff is in Staff. Number 3 means that the Staff is in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please initial this document and also place the date, January 12, 2009.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we still have a translation mistake on page 41, line 25.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So could you please repeat what corresponds to number 2?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Number 2 is "Duty, Chief of Staff." Also deputy commander -- no, no, sorry, 2 is "Staff," staff, organisational unit, staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Could we save this document, please. I would like to return to your report, document 5D759 page 16 in B/C/S and 21 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what is the structure of the Staff, as we see it on this organisational chart in figure 4?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: From the establishment of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and assuming that this establishment is in line with the mobilisation plan, one can see that it is organised at two levels. On the first level is the Administration for Operations and Training and the arms of service, with the information technology service; and at the second level we have the organisational units which are below those of the first level, so that the Administration for Operations and Training has a department for operations, a department for training, and then operations centre, whereas the information technology has an office and a typing pool.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show page 70 to the witness, page 70 in the report in B/C/S, corresponding to page 88 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Here, you wrote that General Miletic was the 6th by rank and the 24th by order in the Republika Srpska. I would like to show you the organisational scheme that we have on the previous page in B/C/S, and English, it's page 88. In B/C/S, it corresponds to page -- to the top of the page. According to this organisational chart which you drew, could you tell us how you were able to determine the rank of General Miletic, as well as the order he had?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: The document concerning the rank and the order of commanding officers in an army is something that almost every army in the world should have. This document is, first of all, important so that position groups can be harmonised, so that replacements can be made, and also for purposes of protocol. Reading the documents linked to this case, I have seen that very often there was a lot of confusion about what commanding officer in the Army of Republika Srpska held what rank. Bearing in mind they had an order on the operation of the Army of Republika Srpska, that they also had the establishment, that I had a large number of orders, I contacted additional interviews with those officers who dealt with organisation within the Army of Republika Srpska and established, on the basis of all this, the precise rank and order in the Army of Republika Srpska. This is the rank at army level, where at first the rank is commander, the second are his assistants and Chief of Staff, or, rather, the chief of staff and assistants. Then the third are the corps commanders; fourth are the chief of staffs of the corps and the commander of the training centre; five, the chiefs of the independent administrations, and five [as interpreted], the chiefs of the administrations, and then I didn't go into any further details. Based on all this, I reached the conclusion presented here. I have checked this diagram with a large number of officers engaged in organisational work, and they all agreed with every detail of this diagram.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to show you document P692. This is another organisational chart, but it is not one you drafted, yourself. Could you please look at this organisational chart of the Main Staff of the VRS, and tell us whether this organisational chart is accurate.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: I expected to see this diagram clearly and precisely in this court, but it's very hard to understand, as are all the documents I've been shown here so far. However, I have managed to decipher much that I needed, and my first conclusion is as follows: The title of this diagram does not correspond with its contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we help him by giving him a hard copy, if this is available? But I think if we have a hard copy, it will make things easier for him. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE

utterances.text: That's a printout out of e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's not a printout out of e-court, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, but the Registrar, Registry has made it. This is harder to read, and I don't think putting it on the ELMO is going to help. What we can do is we can show this to the witness as an aid, and put it on the ELMO in case we need to refer to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness hasn't studied that version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but the variations seem to be minimal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry to be difficult. If the variations are not material, then of course it doesn't matter, but -- THE COURT: Well, I'm not in a position to say whether they are material or not, but I understood Madame Fauveau to indicate that they are not material.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I'm concerned, they are not, but maybe for my colleague, it might be better to use what we have in e-court and then zoom in on some parts as we need them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay, we can do that. I mean, as I said, the whole idea was to provide an aid to the witness. In our case, we can blow up what we have in the e-court, but I don't think that the witness can stay doing that. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we'll make it with the witness, we'll find a way. Don't worry. Could we please zoom the top part of the document in order to see the two first blocks. It might be a complicated exercise, but I'm sure that we will manage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we go through it bit by bit, as we are doing now, and zoom in on the different parts that you need to refer the witness to. I think that can be done without any difficulty at all.

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In these two blocks that you have on the screen, could you tell us whether there are parts that you believe are erroneous?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: One thing I would like to ask you is to zoom in -- or, rather, not to zoom in, but to show me the entire document so I can explain more easily.

utterances.text: Why, perhaps, had you left it there, Madam Registrar --

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, like this, like this. This is what I find appropriate. By Your Honour's leave, could my suggestions be inscribed in this diagram?
