utterances.text: I don't understand that. What do you mean by inscribing your suggestions in this diagram?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to show what is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be easier so the witness can mark where he finds errors, or mistakes, or problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Usher, please, you need to assist the witness to show him how he can mark the document that we have on e-court. Can we zoom in a little bit more. No, no, that's not -- okay, leave it at that. Now, General -- leave it as it is. You can -- all right. You can put any markings that you wish. Fine like that, yeah, leave it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you see the title?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but this one will read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks] My first conclusion was that the diagram does not correspond to its title. The title is "The Structure of the Main Staff of the VRS in July 1995," whereas the contents include units of the Army of Republika Srpska, not its Main Staff. So this is not actually part of this diagram. It shouldn't be here. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because for the record --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because for the record we need to describe what you have done. When the witness made this statement, he crossed out, at the bottom of the document, all the boxes in the last two rows, starting from 1st Krajina Corps to 10th Sabotage Detachment; in total, eight boxes. Yes, we can now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just to be absolutely sure, what has been struck out are 6th Corps, the 65th Protection Regiment and the 10th Sabotage Detachment. Is this what you have struck out and what you wanted to strike out?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: No. All the corps represented here, all the units, they were not within the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. They were subordinate to it, but they were not part of it. So the 1st Corps, the 2nd [indiscernible] Bosniak Corps, the Drina Corps, the Herzegovina Corps, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, the 65th, and the 10th Sabotage Detachment have been crossed out. The next salient point here is that the structure depicted does not correspond to the organisation it has been derived from. The place of the Chief of Staff should be here [Marks], not up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: For things to be clear, could you please draw a cross on the place where the chief of the Main Staff is at the moment on this diagram?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Where it is now or where does it belong?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On this diagram.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: It's here [Marks]. I've marked it with a figure 1, which I've circled. That's where he is. And where he should be is where I've drawn the square.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, General, can he not be there as a deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He is the Chief of Staff and also the deputy commander, but that is a single duty. It cannot be divided into two. All the rights and obligations he has, as deputy commander of the Main Staff, stem from his duty as Chief of Staff, who is also the deputy commander. So pulling him out of his rank like this does not hold water. That's the functional sort of organisational characterized by the NATO forces. That's what's represented here, but that's not the actual situation in the Army of Republika Srpska, which is why there are double lines of command here, but these did not actually exist in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Proceed, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, the regarding the function of the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff, in this box that's not at the right place we see: "Assistant commander and chief of the Main Staff."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: That does not exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just a second, please. You already explained that the function of the chief of the Main Staff does not exist, the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff does not exist; but was General Milovanovic assistant to the commander?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: No, that is incorrect. He was the Chief of Staff, also the deputy commander in the staff of the Main Staff, and his place is where I have depicted it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now -- I would like to know first whether we can zoom in on the organisational chart, as it is. No? That's too bad.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Maybe possibly -- so now at this stage could you please initial the document and place the date, because we will continue with another version of the document. Otherwise, it's going to be too complicated.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: If I may make a suggestion, I would introduce two or three other changes which would not be complicated.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: In addition to this [Marks], these double lines of command, which I am crossing out now [Marks], do not exist. They lead from the Chief of Staff to the other organisational units. And, further, the order of the organisational units is all mixed up. As I've been able to see in the diagram shown a little while ago, there it's in order, so this organisational unit should be in position 6 [Marks]. That's the Administration for the Air Force and Anti-Aircraft Defence. This organisational unit for intelligence and security affairs [Marks] should be in position 4. Only the staff remains in the first place. The organisational unit, I think it says for logistics here, its actual position should be 3 [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just a second. You are at the Department for Moral, Religious and Legal Affairs. That's the box you're at, where you placed the 3; is that it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I heard the translation as referring to logistics, but I think you're right, it needs to be cleared up or clarified.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't see very well. I do apologise. So instead of 3, it should be 2 here, the number 2 [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But he, in the transcript, he had the reference to 3 before. I would have preferred to have the 3 crossed out, rather than have it deleted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next organisational unit, as far as I can see, is for mobilisation and personnel affairs. That should be number 5 [Marks]. That's its correct order. The next -- finally we have logistics here, and it's real place is in position 3 [Marks]. That's the one I crossed out before. And then there's the Administration for Planning and Deployment, and that's 7 [Marks]. So the fact that it's all mixed up here makes it hard to establish the order of the officers, and it also -- it also is not in line with the establishment according to which this diagram was supposed to be drawn up. The next point is that the staff here is called the staff of arms of service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because at least according to the interpretation, you referred to the last box as Administration for Planning and Deployment. In reality, what at least I have on the screen, being the last one, is Department for Development and Finance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. You're right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So number 7 would represent what, then, the Department for Development and Finance or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Administration for Planning and Finance, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, yes, but before the break, because I need to it cleared. If you were to redraw, yourself, this chart therefore, you have moved the box where there is "Milovanovic" right below the "Mladic" box. He would still be number 1, no, Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In that row, yes, he would be number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And then 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. Okay, I think we can have the break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before we take the break, could the witness just sign the document, please, and the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we finished with this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in my understanding, the witness would like to continue, but we can do that after the break, I suppose. But on the same chart, I think that he has a number of changes that he would like to bring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. I leave it up to you, whether to save it now or save it later. It's up to you. Thank you, 25 minutes.

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: All these numbers which you have put above the various boxes and sectors, are these numbers referring to the sectors, or to the heads or chiefs of those sectors, or to both?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: The numbers applies to the sectors, and the segments apply to their heads.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer, as I'm not sure that it has been well recorded.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: The numbers that I placed on this diagram are in reference to the sectors. When they are in reference to the sectors, then they are also in reference to the heads of those sectors.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And could you please now write number 1 above the sector for the staff, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, you said there are also other mistakes in this chart. Could you please tell us what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: At the beginning, I said there was an error in substance, and we dealt with that by doing the drawings on the diagrams. As far as structural errors are concerned, we dealt with that by establishing the order in the diagram. As far as errors with links and relations are concerned, I would just like to say now that these are fictitious links, and whenever there's an X, that's what it means. And there are two types of error that remain. In terms of the nomenclature, what the organisational units are called, and also about not naming the specific duties. I would first like to say something about errors concerning the nomenclature, the names of the organisational units. Each military organisation has the names of units specifically defined, and each unit has a certain rank. In the case at hand, and I'm talking about the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, there are sectors, sectors on an equal level as the staff. You have administrations, departments and sections. The person who produced this diagram put the staff on an equal footing with the branch's staff, but that doesn't exist, and that's the name right here [indicates]. Secondly, this person did not provide a criterion in terms of how he translated the organisational units of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska into English. In my study, I clearly established that criterion. The sectors in the Serbian are sectors in the English. Administrations in the Serbian are departments in the English. And departments, I think we use the word "section" for that. I see that it's not here. In keeping with that, here you have a large number of sectors that are termed administrations or administrations put on an equal footing with sectors. In keeping with this criterion, one needs to establish certain distinctions. The staff remains. Number 2, the Department for Morale, Religion and all that is not a department; rather, it should read "sector." Number 3, again another sector, not a department. Number 4, again "sector," not "department." Number 5, "sector," not "department." Number 6 and number 7 are departments. This name of an organisational unit also applies to the Administration for Training and Operations, and also for the information administration and the security administration. In keeping with this criterion, it is necessary to redraw this diagram, because this is very important in terms of determining the ranks in order to follow. The last part is about appointments or not appointing. I looked at two duties specifically, General Milovanovic first of all. It reads "chef glavno staba," chief of the Main Staff. We've got that clarified and we put an end to that, but then below that it reads "assistant commander, deputy commander." He wasn't a deputy commander. He was the Chief of Staff and also the deputy commander in the operations and teaching administration, it reads, next to General Miletic's [Realtime transcript read in error, "Milutinovic"] name "chief" or "deputy chief." He never was the deputy chief, as a matter of fact. I didn't really check all the other duties well because the diagram and the entire expert report was impossible to scan in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My colleague has pointed out to me that at line 13, there's a reference to General Milutinovic in the record. I believe it should say "General Miletic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. You agree to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, Your Honour, I agree, and I'd like to thank my colleague for that. Now, I think that we can now save this exhibit and that we shall no longer need it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General Kosovac, you said that the administration or "ubrava" in B/C/S should be translated into "department," didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a matter of convention. The standard that we used was that "ubrava" should be translated as "department" and "sektor" remains "sector."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it equally apply to the "ubrava za ONP," which is headed by Mr. Miletic? This should be translated to "Department for Operation and Training"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Department for Operations and Teaching, not for Operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does that unit have the same level as other departments; for example, Department for Mobilisation of Persons and those things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Mobilisation" is "sector," this is the same level as the security department and intelligence department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I had in mind mobilisation, planning and finance or air force department.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The two departments have a higher level than the operations and teaching one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Even if they are using the same terminology, that is, "ubrava"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. These are departments that are at a higher level of organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Madame Fauveau-Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt again. I just want my colleague to clarify or have clarified because there is references to these departments in the expert report that are referred to as "administrations" in the report, and I wonder if we could clarify that. In particular, I could refer to you paragraph 39 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know, as far as I'm concerned, I'd rather translate "ubrava" by "administration" in English, but, you know, this is a linguistic issue. But maybe the witness can use the terms in B/C/S, which will make it easier, and maybe explain the difference between the two administrations at a higher level and the administrations -- and the three other levels of administrations at a lower level, for us to better understand what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The department as an organisational unit, the criterion to establish one, is the sort of business that it transacts and the number of people who are involved, who are members of this unit. It is based on that that you arrive at a conclusion as to whether something constitutes a department or not. However, not all departments are the same. These two departments, the air force and anti-aircraft defence one, and the planning, development and finance one, are placed directly under the commander. They are at a higher organisational level. The remaining three, operations and teaching specifically, the Chief of Staff is in charge, and the security department and the intelligence department under the competence of the assistant commander. It is in such a way that they are placed as a lower level. The difference is clear, and it stems from the difference in rank and order between these departments.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as I'm concerned, I no longer need this chart, and I would like to go back to your report. So again Exhibit 5D759; on page 17 in the B/C/S version, and in English this will be on page 22. And I'm referring to paragraph 43.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In this paragraph, you wrote that the head of administration in charge of operations and training has a right of command over the sections for operations, over the section in charge of training, and over the operations centre. Generally speaking, what is the function of the operations centre?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: The operations centre has a twofold meaning. One meaning denotes an organisational unit, which means there are certain persons working there. The other meaning is about a place where these jobs are performed. Its principle task -- what can be considered its principle task is being the principle mediator between the command links within the army, and this is in relation to the basic command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Was the operation centres formed as part of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: There was supposed to be one, but it wasn't manned, and eventually it wasn't established. The operations centre functioned in such a way that the duty operations officer and the operations centre officer were one and the same, and then various corners were cut. You know that the position of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska was to have maximum manning levels at the lower levels, such as brigades and regiments, and the higher levels should try to operate with as few men as possible, because there was an ongoing shortage of well-trained men to fill these posts.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the fact that there was no operations centre, did that have an impact on the way the department in charge of operations and training functioned?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Well, what is certain is that all the persons working in that department had a lot of other things to do because of this, and all of these were jobs that interfered with their normal work. However, that was the decision that was taken. And as far as I can see, they did quite well coping with the pressure.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the officer for operations who was on duty. What were the tasks of this officer on duty?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: The operative duty officer, because I think that's what we're talking about, within the system is considered the most senior duty officer in an organisational unit. His principal task was, in the commander's absence, to make sure the system was operating in keeping with the orders, plans, and schedules.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And to whom did this duty operations officer report? Who was he subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: The operative duty officer is subordinated to the commander regardless of the fact that sometimes some studies indicate that it's not the commander that dismisses them or replaces them, but rather someone else. Despite this fact, they are directly subordinated to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now I would like to move to another subject and show you page 28 of your report, page 28 in the B/C/S version, which is page 37 -- sorry, 34, 34 in English. Now, what I'm interested in is paragraph 75 in which you wrote, amongst other things, that there was no universal type of military organisation. Can you please explain what you meant by this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: I tried to be as specific as I could. Based on my knowledge of the Army of Republika Srpska, or the VJ, or the Army of Serbia, which I had been a member up until recently, if I tried to explain other military forces based on that, the errors would be disastrous. There is no universal type of organisation. Whenever you deal with an army, you need to analyse it and explain it in its own right, the way it operates, even if you come across two similar ways two armies are organised. If you don't study closely the organisational model of an army but, rather, if you base your analysis on a different if similar model, there is always the risk that you might be committing frightful errors.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Right. May I now come back to page 12 in B/C/S, and I'm still talking about your report, which is page 13 in English. In paragraph 30, you mentioned one particular type of organisation which you called the line staff type of organisation. Can you please explain what this type of organisation comprises? And the chart for the English version is on the following page, which is on page 14.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: It wasn't I who gave these names. It was file in early 19th century, and these are the types of organisation I'm familiar with. The army used the line staff type of organisation. Sometimes one uses the staff-type term, and this has its own features, the features being that among other things, any rights and responsibilities of commander in the hands of a single man, the commander. This is also typical of other types. However, communication only occurs through the commander, meaning if the Chief of Staff of this lower command in the box wants to share something with the Chief of Staff of a superior command, he passes information along through his own commander and then the commander sends it along to his own superior commander, and then the superior commander informs the Chief of Staff. This is the most important difference in relation to all the other types. The hierarchy is solid, it's all linked up, and everything happens through the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And what army had this type of organisation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: The JNA, applied in a very consistent way, and also in all the armies that emerged, as it were, on the ashes of the JNA. It wasn't before the recent years that we switched over to the functional type of organisation, and in the Eastern Bloc countries they also had these, the former Eastern Bloc, but they did have some peculiarities. I don't think we should be going into that type of detail now. They distinguished between the line staff type and the type that they were actually using.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to show you page 13 in the B/C/S version, corresponding to page 16 in the English. In paragraph 33, you talk about another kind of organisation called "functional" or "line functional." Could you give us some explanation on this kind of organisation? The organisational chart in the B/C/S version is on the next page, page 14.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: This is a more advanced aspect of organisation, characterized by a higher level of professionalism of the people working in this system. Regardless of the fact that all the rights, obligations, and executive duties are in the hands of the commander, he can transfer part of his rights and obligations to his assistants; and these assistants have, according to their functional rights, the competence to directly control all their services in depth. This manner of organisation is considered to be more flexible, more efficient, and conducive to speedier decision-making.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell us which armies were organised along this line, along this structure?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: I think almost all armies today, nowadays. At that time, it was mainly the NATO forces that were organised in this way. We adopted this way of organisation in the Serbian Army while I was still in charge of organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just to make things perfectly clear, please tell us what organisation existed in the Army of Republika Srpska in 1995.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: To be very precise, I could say that this line staff type of organisation was used with some admixtures of the functional type of organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You made a parallel between these two organisations and the two types of armies, one being on the Eastern Bloc side and the other on the Western side, so could you tell us whether there was an officer in charge of operations in NATO armies?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: That's the biggest problem. An operative officer of the type has existed in the JNA and the armies that sprang from the JNA does not exist in the NATO system. The entire system of organisation is completely different, so any comparison and any drawing of conclusions based on the other type of organisation leads to error. People who are familiar with the army and organisation of NATO countries equate operations officers with operatives, but this is wrong, both as regards their rights and duties and qualifications and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did the Army of Republika Srpska have a function that could be called adviser to the commander?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: From the code book of duties in the Army of Republika Srpska, which is easy to reconstruct, one can see that adviser -- adviser to the commander or adviser to the chief are positions which do not exist. Studying the orders on competencies, one can see that, in functional terms, in the Army of Republika Srpska and in all the armies coming from the former JNA, there is no advisory function and no counselling of subordinates in relation to their superiors.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you explain this last part of your answer, please? You're saying that there is no advisory function and no counselling of subordinates in relation to their superiors?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: The duty of adviser did not exist, full stop. In the competencies, the activity of giving advice did not exist. This is something that regularly exists in all the armed forces of the NATO countries nowadays.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When General Mladic was absent, could you tell us who, in the Army of Republika Srpska, would fill in for him and stand in for him? Now, of course, before you answer, we have to define exactly what an absence could mean because earlier you already told us about the problems associated with the word "absence." So could you expound on this, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. The microphone was not switched on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you could repeat the list that you were giving of various places, please, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem. Let's state precisely what "absence" means, "Not to be at the command post." If somebody is not present in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, if somebody is not in Han Pijesak, he is not absent from his duty. As long as appropriate communication with him can be established, and as long as he's fit to command, he is on duty. From that point of view, studying all the documents and talking to the people in charge of personnel affairs, the commander of the Army of Republika Srpska was always in command of the Army of Republika Srpska, which means he was never absence from being able to command.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let's assume that General Mladic would not be fit for command or able to command. Who could have stood in for him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Well, it might be easier to refer you to Rule 37 of the Rules of Service, but let me explain. If an emergency arises, a dynamic or sudden situation, a situation which could not be foreseen, then he would be replaced by the most senior officer in the Army of Republika Srpska underneath him, and that was the Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic. If his inability to command occurred in normal conditions, the supreme commander would immediately issue a decision on someone acting for the -- or standing in for the commander until a final decision was reached.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We saw that General Milovanovic's function was to be chief of the -- head of the Main Staff, as well as being deputy commander. You explained -- you told us when General Milovanovic actually stood in for General Mladic, but we know that General Milovanovic signed a great number of documents as deputy commander, so could you explain to us why the deputy commander, General Milovanovic, actually signed these documents in these cases?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC
utterances.text: Studying the voluminous documentation which you put at my disposal, I saw in many places that the chiefs of staff signed documents as deputies of the commander. This was also done by General Milovanovic. In some documents, I saw there was Colonel Krstic at the time, and I saw it on some other documents as well. That is actually an incorrect way of signing because none of them was the deputy of the commander. The duties of the Chief of Staff and deputy commander are an integral whole, so if he was authorised to sign, the correct way would have been to sign it "Chief of Staff and Deputy Commander Colonel Milovanovic." Why they did this, I don't know, and the fact their superiors did not object, they did not feel it was a big problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is this the right time to adjourn?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Fauveau. General, we are going to stop here for today. We'll continue tomorrow. We are going quite slowly, if I may say so. Anyway, between now and tomorrow, please, you're not allowed to discuss with anyone the subject matter of your testimony, and this will continue to be the case until you finish with your evidence sometime next week. Thank you, and adjourned to tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
